Sha'arei Teshuvah 1:41: The Fifteenth Foundation – Prayer: let him pray to the Name and seek mercy that all his iniquities be atoned, as it is said (Hosea 14:3), "Take words with you and return to the Lord; say to Him, Forgive all iniquity, and accept the good, and let us render as bullocks the offering of our lips." "Take words with you and return to the Lord" — this concerns confession. "Say to Him, Forgive all iniquity, and accept the good" — this concerns prayer, and its meaning is: accept the good deed that we have done, for our Sages of blessed memory said that a transgression extinguishes a mitzvah; but at the time of teshuvah the iniquities are atoned, the merit of the mitzvah is awakened, and its lamp shines, after it had not given its light before the teshuvah. And so it is written (Job 8:6), "If you are pure and upright, surely now He will rouse Himself for you and repay the habitation of your righteousness." Our Sages of blessed memory said: it does not say "if you were pure and upright," but "if you are pure and upright" — meaning, that you have done teshuvah; "surely now He will rouse Himself for you" — now, after the teshuvah you have done, He will rouse for you all the acts of charity you performed beforehand, when your house was open wide and you planted a tree of hospitality for wayfarers, as it is written (Job 31:32), "My doors I opened to the traveler" — for before the teshuvah your righteous deeds did not shield you, but after you have returned and your iniquity has departed, He will rouse your merit and repay the habitation of your righteousness. "And let us render as bullocks the offering of our lips" — may He reckon our confession as though it were the sin-offering of bullocks, acceptable before Him; and it mentions bullocks because the sin-offering bullock was an inward one, and some of its blood was sprinkled upon the curtain and upon the golden altar.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 1:42: And further, the penitent should pray to the Name that He wipe away his transgressions like a thick cloud and his sins like a cloud, and that He desire him and be pleased with him and be entreated for him, as though he had not sinned — as is stated in the words of Elihu concerning the penitent after his sufferings (Job 33:26), "he will entreat God and He will be pleased with him." For it is possible for the iniquity to be forgiven and for one to be redeemed from all sufferings and every decree, and yet the Name have no desire in him, and He will not accept an offering from his hand. And the desire of the righteous, among all successes, is to obtain favor from the Name and that He desire them; and His will is life, enduring and true, and the great light that encompasses all delights, as it is said (Psalms 30:6), "life in His favor," and it is said (Psalms 80:20), "O Lord God of hosts, cause Your face to shine, and we shall be saved." And our Sages of blessed memory said: we have nothing but the shining of Your face — and that is the matter of favor, as we have already stated and explained earlier. Therefore you will see in David's prayer at the time of his teshuvah, after he said (Psalms 51:4), "Wash me thoroughly of my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin," that he prayed further concerning the favor, that the will of the Blessed Name be toward him as before the sin, and he said (Psalms 51:13), "Cast me not away from Your presence, and take not Your holy spirit from me." After that he prayed and said (Psalms 51:14), "Restore to me the joy of Your salvation" — that the miracles of the Name and His salvation be found with him, and that the spirit of God prosper upon him as at first. And after that he said (ibid.), "and let a generous spirit sustain me." Its meaning: behold, I have become small because of my transgression, and I am not worthy of Your miracles and that Your holy arm be revealed upon me; and even if You have forgiven the iniquity of my sin, I am not worthy to be loved and favored as in months past — but sustain me with a generous spirit, for there is no limit to Your generosity and Your goodness; and "ve-ruach" is written with the letter bet omitted, as in (Genesis 27:37), "and grain and wine I have sustained him (semachtiv)" [i.e. semachtiv b'ruach]. And in this matter Hosea, peace upon him, said (Hosea 14:5), "I will heal their backsliding, I will love them freely (nedavah)" — the matter of "I will love them freely" is like what David said, "[and a generous (nedivah) spirit] shall sustain me."
Sha'arei Teshuvah 1:43: And further, the penitent should pray always to the Lord that He help him toward teshuvah, as it is said (Jeremiah 31:18), "Turn me back, and I shall return, for You are the Lord my God."
Sha'arei Teshuvah 1:44: The Sixteenth Foundation – Setting Right What Was Twisted, Wherever He Is Able to Set It Right: as it is said (Jonah 3:10), "And God saw their deeds, that they turned from their evil way," and it is said (Jonah 3:8), "and let them turn, every man from his evil way and from the violence that is in their hands." For in matters between a man and his fellow, such as robbery and violence, his iniquity is not atoned until he restores the stolen object; and likewise if he distressed his fellow and pressed upon him, or shamed his face, or spoke evil speech about him, he has no atonement until he seeks forgiveness from him. And so our Sages of blessed memory said, that even though he has already paid him the compensation for his shame and for the pain of the blow, the pain of the shame and the blow is not forgiven him until he seeks [forgiveness] from him, as it is said (Genesis 20:7), "Now restore the man's wife, for he is a prophet, and he will pray for you, and you shall live."
Sha'arei Teshuvah 1:45: And it is fitting for the penitent to do this before his confession, so that his confession find favor. And David the king, peace upon him, did so at the time of his teshuvah, before his confession, as it is said (Psalms 51:6), "Against You, You alone, have I sinned, and done what is evil in Your eyes; that You may be justified when You speak, and be found blameless when You judge." Its meaning: against You alone am I reckoned a sinner, and I need nothing but Your forgiveness; for if I had sinned against a man, I would already have sought his forgiveness and made atonement to him — as in (Genesis 43:9), "then let me bear the blame before my father forever" — meaning, for this sin I shall be reckoned a sinner before my father forever, for regarding this he will not forgive me (its Targum renders: "and I shall be a sinner to my father"); or the meaning of "against You alone have I sinned" may be: I have not sinned against any man, nor spoken presumptuously against him, nor taken anything at all from any man's hand for which I would need his forgiveness and to restore what was stolen; my atonement depends on nothing but Your forgiveness. "That You may be justified when You speak, and be found blameless when You judge" — in order to show the nations Your righteousness and the greatness of Your forgiveness, on the day of Your word and Your law, at the time You judge me. And the term "that" (l'ma'an) is used because the greatness of the sin is the cause by which the greatness of the righteousness in His forgiveness becomes known; therefore the matter is treated as though it were the very purpose from the start — that the kindness of the Name and His righteousness in forgiving be revealed on the day He judges. And likewise (Hosea 8:4), "their silver and their gold they have made into idols for themselves, that it may be cut off" — for the making of idols is the cause of the cutting off of their silver and gold, yet the matter is described as though they made the idols for the purpose of being cut off. Or its meaning may be: for this reason, You will be justified in Your speech concerning the reckoning and the payment (meaning, that he justifies the Blessed One's judgment upon himself); and likewise "that it may be cut off" means "for this reason it will be cut off."
Sha'arei Teshuvah 1:46: And in this first manner our Sages of blessed memory explained, in the Midrash on Psalms: a parable of a physician who saw the wound and said, How very great is this wound! Said the patient: But surely this grievous wound I was struck with was only in order that the righteousness of your cure be revealed, and in order to show your skill! And we shall add further instruction on this foundation in the Fourth Gate.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 1:47: The Seventeenth Foundation – To Pursue the Practice of Kindness and Truth: as it is said (Proverbs 16:6), "Through kindness and truth iniquity is atoned, and through the fear of the Lord one turns from evil." Now consider the deep meaning of this verse. Is it really true that if the sinner has not returned to the Lord, his iniquity will not be atoned through an act of kindness? — as it is said (Deuteronomy 10:17), "who shows no favor and takes no bribe." And our Sages of blessed memory explained: He does not take the bribe of a mitzvah to forgive and to overlook iniquities. They further said: whoever says the Holy One, blessed be He, is lenient — his life will be forfeited; rather, He is slow to anger, but if people do not heed, He measures out their deeds into their own bosom. Rather, this saying of Solomon the king, peace upon him, "through kindness and truth iniquity is atoned," speaks of the penitent, for there are transgressions for which teshuvah and Yom Kippur suspend atonement and sufferings scour it away, as will be explained in the Fourth Gate; and behold, kindness shields the sinner and protects him from suffering, since even mere shade can save from death, as it is written (Proverbs 10:2), "but righteousness (charity) delivers from death." And there is yet another iniquity, the iniquity of desecrating the Name, for which teshuvah and suffering suspend atonement, and death alone scours it away, as it is said (Isaiah 22:14), "Surely this iniquity shall not be forgiven you until you die." Now, when a person strives to support the hand of truth, and helps it forward and is roused by its words, and his light shines before the eyes of the people, and he strengthens the hands of men of truth and lifts up their heads, while he brings low the factions of falsehood and reduces them to dust — behold, these are ways of sanctifying the Name, glory and majesty for His faith and service in the world, and strength and splendor in the sanctuary of His Torah; therefore, by multiplying his acts to sanctify the Name and to rouse the truth, to establish it and support it, he is forgiven for the iniquity of desecration together with his teshuvah, since he has set truth against the guilt of the desecration — the measure of his teshuvah against the measure of his backsliding. This is the explanation of "through kindness and truth iniquity is atoned."
Sha'arei Teshuvah 1:48: The Eighteenth Foundation – That His Sin Be Ever Before Him: for it befits the sinning soul to remember its iniquities always, and not forget them ("teshi" meaning "forget") to the end of its days, and they should not be snatched from his heart until the day of his passing, as it is said (Psalms 51:5), "For I know my transgressions, and my sin is ever before me." And this foundation will be explained in the Third Gate.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 1:49: The Nineteenth Foundation – Abandoning His Sin When It Comes Within His Reach While He Is in the Full Strength of His Desire: and our Sages of blessed memory said (Yoma 86b): Who is the penitent whose teshuvah reaches even to the Throne of Glory? One who is tested and comes out unblemished at the same time, in the same place, and with the same woman — meaning, the sin came within his reach and he was in the full strength of his inclination and his vigor was in his loins just as at the first time he sinned, yet he subdued his inclination and escaped iniquity out of fear of the Name and the awe of his dread of Him. And one to whom the matter has not come within reach in this way should add the fear of the Name to his soul day by day, continually, all his days; and when he has replaced the power that was sufficient to subdue his inclination with this power in such measure that it rules over the full force of the desire — He who examines hearts will understand it, and He who guards the soul will know it, that if he should come to be tested and it should come within his reach as in the first instance, he would save his soul from the hand of his inclination; and behold, he stands before the Lord at the highest level of teshuvah. And this is what Solomon the king, peace upon him, said (Proverbs 16:6), "through kindness and truth iniquity is atoned, and through the fear of the Lord one turns from evil" — its meaning: through the fear of the Lord, to turn from evil should it come within his reach (the word "sur," "to turn," being an infinitive). And proof for this interpretation is that it does not say "ve-sur" ("and turn"); and what is said (Psalms 34:15), "Turn from evil and do good," (Job 1:1), "and feared God, and turned from evil" — their meaning is that he turns from the evil when it comes within his reach, for one would not simply say "turn from a deed" except regarding one who comes close to doing it. And our Sages of blessed memory said in the Midrash: one who sat and did not commit a transgression is given reward as one who performed a mitzvah — as when a matter of transgression came within his reach and he was saved from it.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 1:50: The Twentieth Foundation – To Turn Many Back from Iniquity, As Far As His Ability Reaches: as it is said (Ezekiel 18:30), "Repent, and turn yourselves back from all your transgressions," from which we learn that this is among the foundations of teshuvah; and it is said (Leviticus 19:17), "You shall surely rebuke your fellow, and not bear sin because of him," from which we learn that if he does not rebuke him, he will be punished for his sins. And David the king, peace upon him, said in the psalm of teshuvah (Psalms 51:15), "I will teach transgressors Your ways, and sinners shall return to You."
Sha'arei Teshuvah 1:51: Now we have completed the explanation of the foundations of teshuvah. And now, take to heart to consider the things that hinder teshuvah — meaning, that whoever throws off restraint and continually stumbles in one of them finds his teshuvah difficult. If you have continually stumbled in one of them, be strong and courageous to pour out your speech and multiply prayer and supplication, and gird yourself with strength to fulfill every one of the foundations of teshuvah, and add further instruction concerning them from the ways that will be explained in the Fourth Gate, and you will find favor and be granted mercy.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 1:52: I will mention to you some of what our Sages spoke of in this regard. Our Sages of blessed memory said: twenty-four things hinder teshuvah, and these are they: talebearing and evil speech; a man of wrath; one who harbors evil thoughts; one who attaches himself to a wicked man; one accustomed to a meal that does not suffice its hosts; one who gazes at forbidden sights; one who shares with a thief; one who says, I will sin and then repent — and so they said in the Mishnah: one who says, I will sin and then repent, is not given the opportunity to do teshuvah; I will sin and Yom Kippur will atone — Yom Kippur does not atone [for such a one]; one who honors himself through his fellow's disgrace; one who separates himself from the community; one who demeans his parents; one who demeans his teachers; one who curses the community; one who prevents the community from performing a mitzvah; one who turns his fellow from a good way to an evil way; one who makes use of a poor man's pledge; one who accepts a bribe in order to pervert others in judgment; one who finds a lost object and does not return it to its owner; one who sees his son in bad ways and does not protest against it; one who consumes the spoil of the poor, orphans, and widows; one who disputes the words of the Sages; one who suspects the innocent; one who hates rebuke; and one who mocks the commandments.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 2:1:
Gate Two – To Teach the Paths by Which a Person Is Aroused to Return to the Lord.
Know that the paths of the causes by which a person is aroused to turn back from his evil ways are six. And through each of them we have taught a person understanding of how to divide his own inquiry into his own nature and give ear to his own disposition; and we open for them an ear to hear, to understand and to know precious foundations, sought out and examined for all their purposes. And more than these, my son, be careful to return every day and to purify your soul, without waiting to see an arousing cause and letting the events of the day ensnare your thoughts; for when you remember your Creator, the remembrance of Him will restore your soul from the natural ways of a clod of dust, and thus, though bare, you will awaken the bow of knowledge to straighten the crookedness of your nature, and through the fear of the Name and love of Him and shame before Him you will always add to your rank, and you will be diligent in the cleanness of your hands and cut off rebellious thoughts from your musings, and the vessel-bearers of your soul will be purified; and in remembering its Maker, the soul will don its ornaments and perfect its beauty, as it is written (Isaiah 45:25), "In the Lord shall all the seed of Israel be justified and shall glory." And you should add courage to awaken your spirit through the paths of the six causes that will be explained. But whoever has not attained this rank, his uncircumcised heart submits itself only by way of causes and by seeing much — and according to the paucity of recognition through the arousing cause that moves a person's heart to teshuvah, and according to its tendency toward the way of ready will, one may know and discern that the teshuvah comes from a worthy soul.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 2:2: The First Path – when troubles find a man, let him take it to heart and say, This is nothing but the result of my own ways and my own deeds, which have brought these upon me, and my sins have wrought harm to my own soul; and let him return to the Lord, and He will have mercy on him — as it is said (Deuteronomy 31:17), "and many evils and troubles shall find him, and he shall say on that day, Is it not because my God is not in my midst that these evils have found me?" And you will see, according to the custom of flesh and blood, that if a man sins against another, and at the time of his own trouble he regrets it and submits to him because he needs his help — this regret will appear inferior in his fellow's eyes, as Jephthah said (Judges 11:7), "Why have you come to me now, when you are in distress?" But it is among the kindnesses of the Blessed Name that He accepts teshuvah that comes from the midst of trouble, and it becomes acceptable before Him; and He shall love the sinner freely, when he returns to Him on the day of rebuke and out of the midst of trouble, as it is said (Hosea 14:2-3), "Return, O Israel, to the Lord your God, for you have stumbled in your iniquity. Take words with you... I will heal their backsliding, I will love them freely." And it is said (Proverbs 3:12), "For whom the Lord loves He rebukes, even as a father the son in whom he delights." But if the man does not turn back from his evil way on the day of evil, and is rebuked through pain and does not turn back to the one who rebukes him, his iniquity will grow and his punishment be doubled. Behold, if a king chastises one who has sinned against him and he is not corrected, the king will harden his discipline and make his yoke very much heavier; and it is written (Leviticus 26:18), "And if, for all this, you will not listen to Me, then I will chastise you seven times more for your sins," and it is said (Job 36:13), "but the impious of heart lay up wrath; they cry not when He binds them." And if a man neither knows nor considers that his troubles have found him because of his sins, but rather says, as the Philistines said (I Samuel 6:9), "it was not His hand that struck us, it was a chance that happened to us" — then wrath will be upon him before the Lord, and the iniquity of this faction will be greater than the sin of the first faction. Therefore it is written first, of the first faction, "then I will chastise you seven times more," and afterward it is written of the other, mentioned faction (Leviticus 26:21), "And if you walk contrary to Me, and are not willing to listen to Me..." — for the whole of the latter faction in that passage is more severe than the first. And afterward it is written (ibid.), "And if for these things you will not be corrected unto Me, but will walk contrary to Me, then I also will walk contrary to you," and after that it is written (ibid.), "And if in this you will not listen to Me, but walk contrary to Me, then I will walk contrary to you in the fury of contrariness." And its meaning: "you will walk contrary to Me," for you will say, it was a chance that happened to us. And if a man does not recognize his own deeds and does not know that iniquity is in his hand, from having sinned, it is upon him to search through his deeds and examine his ways, as it is said (Lamentations 3:40), "Let us search and examine our ways." And if he closes his eyes and his thoughts are made foolish and grow proud, and he does not scrutinize his ways nor know the work of his hands and what his fingers have wrought, and says, I have not sinned — his sin has grown very heavy, as it is said (Jeremiah 2:35), "Behold, I will bring you to judgment, because you say, I have not sinned," and it is said (Isaiah 42:25), "and it burned him all around, yet he did not know; it consumed him, yet he did not lay it to heart," and it is said (Proverbs 19:3), "The foolishness of a man perverts his way, and his heart frets against the Lord."
Sha'arei Teshuvah 2:3: And know and understand that the Blessed Name's chastisement is for man's own good, for if a man has sinned before Him and done evil in His eyes, the Name's chastisement upon him serves two purposes. The first, to atone for his sins and remove his iniquity, as it is said (Psalms 25:18), "Look upon my affliction and my toil, and forgive all my sins" — and through the bodily illnesses with which the Lord has afflicted him, He heals the sickness of his soul, for iniquity is the sickness of the soul, as it is said (ibid. 41:5), "Heal my soul, for I have sinned against You," and it is said (Isaiah 33:24), "And no inhabitant shall say, I am sick; the people who dwell there shall be forgiven their iniquity." And the second purpose, to remind him and to turn him back from his evil ways, as it is written (Zephaniah 3:7), "Surely you will fear Me, you will accept discipline." And if he does not accept the discipline, nor is at ease because of the rebuke, and does not circumcise the foreskin of his heart — woe to him and woe to his soul, for he has borne suffering and carried his iniquity, and yet his iniquity is not accepted, but his punishment is doubled, as we have explained.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 2:4: And when a person accepts the Name's chastisement and improves his ways and his deeds, it is fitting for him to rejoice in his sufferings, since they have benefited him with sublime benefits, and he ought to thank the exalted Name for them just as for all his other successes, as it is said (Psalms 116:13), "I will lift up the cup of salvations, and call upon the name of the Lord," and it is said (ibid. 116:3-4), "Trouble and sorrow I found, and I called upon the name of the Lord." And our Sages of blessed memory said in the Sifrei: Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov says, as long as a person is at ease, none of his iniquities are atoned; but through suffering he becomes acceptable to the Omnipresent, as it is said (Proverbs 3:12), "For whom the Lord loves He rebukes, even as a father the son in whom he delights." Its meaning: just as a father favors the son [whom he rebukes], so does the Lord favor the one whom He has rebuked and who has accepted His discipline — in the manner that a father favors his son after rebuking him. And one may explain further: "even as a father rebukes the son in whom he delights," and he does not rebuke sons whom he has despaired of and knows that rebuke will not benefit them; and this is said of people who do not recognize the benefit and value of rebuke, as it is written (Hosea 7:13), "though I would redeem them, they have spoken lies against Me," and it is said (Hosea 7:15), "though I have disciplined them and strengthened their arms, yet they devise evil against Me," and it is said (Hosea 11:3), "and I taught Ephraim to walk, taking them by their arms, but they did not know that I healed them."
Sha'arei Teshuvah 2:5: And one who trusts in the Name should hope even in the swift passing of his distress, for the darkness will become the cause of the light, as it is written (Micah 7:8), "Rejoice not against me, O my enemy; though I have fallen, I shall rise; though I sit in darkness, the Lord is a light to me." And our Sages of blessed memory said: had I not fallen, I would not have risen; had I not sat in darkness, there would have been no light for me. And every single man, on the day of his distress, should set his heart to understand and to afflict himself with teshuvah and prayer, just as the community is obligated to fast and afflict itself in the time of its trouble, as our Sages of blessed memory instituted, and this is a chosen fast and a day of favor. And when the Blessed Name's chastisement comes upon a man who is pure and upright, it is a trial, and it will increase his reward in the World to Come, as it is said (Deuteronomy 8:16), "to afflict you and to test you, to do you good in your latter end." And our Sages of blessed memory said: one who searches his deeds at the time of his trouble, and examines and investigates and finds no sin in his hand — these are truly sufferings of love.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 2:6: And of this path which we have mentioned is teshuvah on the day of death, when the sinner sees that evil has come to its full measure against him and his hope is lost, as it is written (Proverbs 11:7), "When a wicked man dies, hope is lost"; and he confesses at that time and returns to the Lord with a whole heart. And even this teshuvah is of avail, though it does not reach the level of the teshuvah of one who returns in the full innocence of his strength, as we stated earlier in the First Gate.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 2:7: The Second Path – when the days of old age come and the days of gray hair arrive, and his strength fails and diminishes, and his inclination is bowed down — let him also remember his end, that it is near, and understand his latter days, and return to the Lord, and He will have mercy on him. But whoever does not return in teshuvah when the days of old age come, his punishment is doubled and great is the wrath against him, as our Sages of blessed memory said: there are three whom the Holy One, blessed be He, hates — the poor man who is haughty, the rich man who denies [his obligations], and the old man who commits adultery. And it is said (Hosea 7:9), "Strangers have devoured his strength, and he knows it not; gray hairs also are sprinkled upon him, and he knows it not." And it is a matter of astonishment and wonder that a man stands at the midpoint of his days and sees that the days are diminishing, and the demolition of the structure has begun, and what nature grasped is now lacking, and dryness is seen in it, as it is said (Psalms 102:12), "My days are like a lengthening shadow, and I am withered like grass" — how is it that his eyes are plastered over and his heart fails to comprehend, and he does not see that he is journeying to the place, the place of his eternal home, traveling and journeying, day and night?
Sha'arei Teshuvah 2:8: And there are many people from whom the light of teshuvah is withheld, because they are innocent and pure in their own eyes and do not bestir themselves to correct their deeds, for they have imagined about themselves that they are upright, while they have sinned very greatly against the Lord. Is it not written (Ecclesiastes 7:20), "For there is no righteous man on earth who does good and does not sin"? And these people, because they belittle the matter of sins, do not feel it or understand it — or their sin is made known to them, and afterward it is forgotten from their heart; and they are like a sick man who does not feel his sickness and does not think about a cure, and his sickness continually grows heavier until he can no longer be cured. And sometimes the cause of this is the shortness of their understanding, for they do not come to seek God, and they have no desire to know His ways; therefore they are not diligent at the doors of the wise and their disciples, as it is said (Proverbs 15:12), "A scoffer loves not to be rebuked; he will not go to the wise."
Sha'arei Teshuvah 2:9: Now, there are righteous and upright men in their own hearts who continually roar like a lion in their thoughts, and moan over their sins like the roaring of the sea, over their falling short in the service of the Name — for concerning this a man transgresses and multiplies guilt just as with grave transgressions, as our Sages of blessed memory said: the Holy One, blessed be He, overlooked sexual immorality and bloodshed, but did not overlook the iniquity of neglecting Torah study. This is so even though the world is full of people whose thoughts and deeds are focused mainly on the desires of their body and the vanities of their time, and into whose souls the secret of fear does not enter, and who do not search their innermost being about it; whose glory finds no rest in the imagery of their hearts, their inner chambers, and their imagination at set times; who give no portion of their affairs to Torah; and from whose innermost heart the reckoning of their soul is lost, for they are a nation void of counsel — how much more, then, are these people [who abandon Torah study] on a lower level. And our Sages of blessed memory said: at sixty, one reaches old age; at seventy, gray hair; at eighty, special strength; at ninety, one is bent over [or: given to meditation]; at one hundred, it is as though he were already dead and had passed on and ceased from the world. And the intent of our Sages, of blessed memory, in these words was to warn concerning teshuvah, that a man should think about his end when he reaches the days of old age, if he did not merit to do so in the days of his youth; and since his time draws near, he should abandon the desires and cravings of the body and set his soul in order. And upon reaching the days of gray hair, he should further banish the affairs of this world from his heart; and according to the diminishing years that remain to him, he should lessen his engagement in worldly matters, and set himself apart continually to reflect on the fear of the Name, to take account with his own soul, to correct his character traits, and to seek out Torah and the commandments. And what they said, "at ninety, one is given to meditation (lasuach)," is in the sense of (Psalms 102:1), "he pours out his meditation (sicho)," (Genesis 24:63), "to meditate in the field (lasuach basadeh)" — as our Sages of blessed memory explained, that Isaac instituted the Minchah prayer, as it is said, "And Isaac went out to meditate in the field"; for after reaching ninety, it is fitting for a man that his whole occupation be prayers and praises of the Name and meditation on His wonders. And Solomon the king, peace upon him, spoke concerning the days of old age, that a man should not grow lazy in them in the service of the Blessed Name, and said (Ecclesiastes 11:6), "In the morning sow your seed, and in the evening do not withhold your hand, for you do not know which will succeed, this or that, or whether both alike will be good." He compared the days of childhood and youth to the morning, and the days of old age to the evening; and the seed is a figure for sons and disciples, as our Sages of blessed memory said: if you married in your youth, marry also in your old age; if you raised disciples in your youth, raise disciples also in your old age — for perhaps the children of your old age will succeed more in Torah and mitzvot than the children of your youth, and likewise the disciples he raises in his old age may perhaps succeed more than the earlier ones, or both alike will be good. Afterward it says (Ecclesiastes 11:7), "And the light is sweet, and it is good for the eyes to see the sun." Its meaning: he returns to speak of the days of old age, which he compared to the evening; and because the old man does not taste what he eats and drinks, as in the words of Barzillai the Gileadite, he says that it befits the old man to take pleasure in the light of the sun, and let him not become impatient with it — for impatience prevents a man from the work of Heaven; and the light will become sweet to him when he weighs it against the days of darkness that are coming, as he mentions further below in the verse (Ecclesiastes 11:8), "But if a man live many years, let him rejoice in them all, yet let him remember the days of darkness, for they shall be many; all that comes is vanity." Its meaning: even should a man grow very old, let him not become a burden to himself, but let him rejoice in all his years, so as not to lose even one of his years and not cease from the service of the Creator; and let him remember the days of darkness, for they will be many, and then he will no longer be able to perform the service, as it is said (Psalms 6:6), "in the grave, who shall give You thanks?" And the righteous grow stronger in their old age and gird themselves with strength and renew their vigor for the service of the Name, as our Sages of blessed memory said: the disciples of the wise, the older they grow, the more wisdom increases in them, and it is said (Psalms 92:15), "They shall still bring forth fruit in old age; they shall be full of sap and green," and it mentions earlier (Psalms 92:13-14), "The righteous shall flourish like the palm tree... planted in the house of the Lord," for the righteous are planted in the house of the Lord from their youth and grow up in the houses of study from their young manhood, like the palm that flourishes and the cedar that grows in Lebanon. And so our Sages of blessed memory said: "planted in the house of the Lord" — these are the children [brought there from infancy], in the manner of what is written (Psalms 144:12), "that our sons may be like plants grown up in their youth." And it says further concerning this matter that they are not to be compared to trees in this respect, for trees, as they grow old, give no more of their strength, while the righteous "shall still bring forth fruit in old age." David the king, peace upon him, also said further (Psalms 71:18), "Now also when I am old and grayheaded, O God, forsake me not, until I have declared Your strength to this generation, and Your might to every one that is to come."
Sha'arei Teshuvah 2:10: The Third Path – when he hears the chastisement of the wise and of those who rebuke, let him listen and hear and submit and return in teshuvah, and accept in his heart all the words of rebuke without diminishing anything from them. And behold, this man, in a single brief moment, comes out of darkness into a great light; for at the time he gives ear and attends, and his heart understands and turns back and accepts, on the day he hears the words of the one who rebukes him, and he resolves upon himself to do all that those who uphold the Torah instruct him from that day forward, to be careful just as those who possess understanding of the times warn him — teshuvah has come into his hand and he has become another man. And from the moment he accepted this in his mind and resolved this in his heart, he has acquired for his soul merit and reward for all the commandments and all the ethical teachings, and fortunate is he, for he has made his soul righteous in a brief hour. And so our Sages of blessed memory said (Mekhilta, Exodus 12:28), "And the children of Israel went and did" — did they do it immediately? Did they not in fact not do it until the fourteenth of the month? Rather, once they accepted upon themselves to do it, Scripture reckons it to them as though they had already done it immediately. And it is said in the Avot of Rabbi Natan: whoever's deeds exceed his wisdom, his wisdom endures, as it is said (Exodus 24:7), "We will do and we will hear." The explanation of the matter is that a man who accepts upon his soul, with a faithful heart, to keep and to do according to the Torah as he shall be instructed, and according to the ruling that those who sit in judgment shall tell him — he has from this very day reward for all the commandments, both for what his ear has already heard of the words of Torah and understood, and for the matters his ear has not yet had revealed to it; he has clothed himself in righteousness and acquired merit both for what is revealed to him and for all that is still hidden from his eyes. And after this he shall seek, day by day, and be diligent at the doors of those who rebuke him, and gain understanding from all who teach him. And thus this man's deeds are found to exceed his wisdom, for he did not yet know the matter, and yet his reward is already his — in the manner of what Israel said at Sinai, "We will do and we will hear," for they placed the acceptance of the deed upon their souls before the hearing. In any other manner, it would not be possible for a man's deeds to exceed what he knows.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 2:11: And whoever is not aroused by the voice of those who rebuke him — his iniquity is doubled, for they warned him and he hardened his heart and was not careful, as it is said (Proverbs 17:10-11), "A rebuke enters deeper into a man of understanding than a hundred blows into a fool. A rebellious man seeks only evil, and a cruel messenger shall be sent against him." Its meaning: the evil man does not submit to the voice of those who rebuke him, but seeks to rebel; and because he was not corrected by the words of the rebuking messenger, a cruel messenger shall be sent against him, measure for measure — for those who rebuke are called messengers (angels), as it is said (II Chronicles 36:16), "But they mocked the messengers of God, and despised His words, and scoffed at His prophets." And Solomon the king, peace upon him, further said (Proverbs 15:10), "Grievous discipline is for him who forsakes the way; he who hates rebuke shall die." Its meaning: true, grievous discipline is fitting for one who forsakes the way and transgresses the words of the Torah, yet there is hope that he may be corrected and turn back from his evil way; but worse than he is one who hates rebuke, for he has no hope or remedy through grievous discipline, but his sentence is only to die — for one who commits a transgression, desire has overpowered him and his inclination has seduced him, and it is possible that his soul is bitter to him that he did not restrain his strength before his inclination, and perhaps he longs for rebuke and hopes for discipline; but one who hates rebuke has already despaired of his own soul, and his hatred of rebuke will testify against him that he hates the words of the Blessed Name.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 2:12: Solomon the king, peace upon him, further said (Proverbs 15:30-31), "The light of the eyes rejoices the heart; a good report makes the bones fat. An ear that hears the rebuke of life shall abide among the wise." And every wise-hearted person should know that it is inconceivable that Solomon the king, peace upon him, would have composed such empty words for no purpose in the midst of words of ethical instruction and fear of the Lord, since Scripture already testifies of him (I Kings 4[5]:11), "and he was wiser than all men." Rather, this is the meaning of the matter: "The light of the eyes rejoices the heart" — the eye is a most honorable organ, for through it one sees the luminaries that rejoice the heart; and more honorable than it is the ear, for through it one hears a good report that makes fat the bone, which has no feeling and is not made fat by the light of the eyes except through an added pleasure. And so our Sages of blessed memory said that the ear is more honorable than the other organs, for if one blinded another's eye, he pays him the value of his eye, but if he deafened him, he pays him the value of his whole self. And behold, a person is obligated to serve the Blessed Name with all his organs and faculties, for it was for His service that He formed them, as it is written (Proverbs 16:4), "The Lord has made everything for its own purpose" — how much more so with the honorable organs He formed in him is he obligated to serve his Maker through them. And the punishment is far greater if he keeps them from the performance of the commandments and does not serve through them, and does not repay in kind for them — for the Lord has done him great good through his honorable senses, and crowned him with honor and majesty through them. Therefore he mentioned first one of the merits of the ear, in order to show you the greatness of the obligation of His service, and explained afterward that the service of the ear consists in listening to rebukes, and he said, "An ear that hears the rebuke of life shall abide among the wise." Its meaning: it is fitting for it to dwell among the wise, after it has listened attentively to their rebuke. And our Sages of blessed memory said: if a man fell from the roof and his limbs were broken, he needs a bandage and dressing for each and every one of his limbs and each of his bones; but the sinner who sinned with all his limbs is considered as though a wound had spread over all his limbs, from the sole of his foot to his crown, as it is said (Isaiah 1:6), "From the sole of the foot even to the head there is no soundness in it." And behold, the Holy One, blessed be He, heals all his limbs with a single bandage, and that is the hearing of the ear, as it is said (Isaiah 55:3), "Incline your ear, and come to Me; hear, and your soul shall live."
Sha'arei Teshuvah 2:13: The Fourth Path – when a man meditates on the Torah of the Lord and reads the words of the Prophets and the Writings, and comprehends the pleasantness of the ethical teachings, and sees the warnings and the punishments — he will tremble at the words and prepare his heart to better his ways and his deeds, and he will find favor with the Name, as it is said (Isaiah 66:2), "and to this one I will look, to the poor and of a contrite spirit, and who trembles at My word." And so it is written concerning Josiah (II Kings 22:11), "And it came to pass, when the king heard the words of the book of the Torah, that he tore his garments." And concerning Ezra it is said (Nehemiah 8:9), "For all the people wept when they heard the words of the Torah." But whoever does not set his heart to the words of the Lord, his transgression grows heavy upon him, as it is said (Jeremiah 36:24), "Yet they were not afraid, nor did they tear their garments." And our Sages of blessed memory said: whoever studies but does not fulfill, it would have been better for him had his afterbirth been turned over upon his face and he never emerged into the air of the world. And it is said (Hosea 8:12), "I write for him the great things of My Torah, but they are counted as a strange thing," and it is said (Jeremiah 8:8), "How do you say, We are wise, and the Torah of the Lord is with us? Surely, behold, the false pen of the scribes has made it into falsehood."
Sha'arei Teshuvah 2:14: The Fifth Path – during the Ten Days of Repentance. Let one who fears the word of the Name feel trembling within himself, knowing that all his deeds are written in the book, and that at that time God will bring every deed into judgment, concerning everything hidden, whether good or evil — for a man is judged on Rosh Hashanah and his sentence is sealed on Yom Kippur. And when he knows that his case will be brought before a king of flesh and blood, will he not tremble with great trembling, and take counsel with himself, and hasten by every diligent means to find himself a way of escape? And it should not occur to him to turn aside to the right or to the left, or to occupy himself with his other pursuits; he should not concern himself with opening and tilling his ground, nor turn toward his vineyards, nor grow slack on the day of distress from preparing his heart to be delivered like a gazelle from the hand [of the hunter]. Therefore, how foolish are those who go out to their labor and their business until evening in these awesome days, the days of judgment and law, while not knowing what their judgment will be! Should not their hearts meditate upon themselves on the day when they will be spoken of, as it is said (Song of Songs 8:8), "What shall we do for our sister on the day when she shall be spoken for?" And it befits every God-fearing person to lessen his affairs so that his thoughts may be settled, and to set aside times, day and night, to seclude himself in his chambers and search and examine his ways, to rise early for the night watches and occupy himself with the ways of teshuvah and the improvement of his deeds, and to pour out speech and lift up prayer and song and to offer supplication. And this is a time of favor, and prayer is heard in it, as it is said (Isaiah 49:8), "In a time of favor I have answered you, and in a day of salvation I have helped you." And our Sages of blessed memory said (Rosh Hashanah 18a): "Seek the Lord while He may be found" — these are the ten days between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur. And it is a positive commandment of the Torah for a man to awaken his spirit to return in teshuvah on Yom Kippur, as it is said (Leviticus 16:30), "from all your sins before the Lord shall you be purified." Therefore Scripture warned us that we be purified before the Lord through our teshuvah, and He will atone for us on this day, to purify us.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 2:15: The Sixth Path – at every moment let him be prepared to meet his God, for a man does not know his time; therefore let him search his innermost being and set himself right through righteousness, to return his spirit in purity to the God who gave it, and let him search his ways and his deeds every day, examining them each morning and testing them at every moment. And our Sages of blessed memory said: Rabbi Eliezer says, Repent one day before your death. His disciples said to him, Our teacher, does a man then know on which day he will die? He said to them, All the more reason let him repent today, lest he die tomorrow — and so all his days will be found spent in teshuvah. And it says (Ecclesiastes 9:8), "At all times let your garments be white, and let your head lack no oil." The whiteness of the garments is a figure for the cleanness of the soul through teshuvah, and the oil is a figure for good deeds and a good name. Our Sages of blessed memory further said, on this matter, a parable of a sailor's wife who was adorning herself, applying kohl to her eyes, while her husband was crossing the seas; and her neighbors said to her, Has not your husband gone far away on a journey — why then do you needlessly beautify yourself? She said to them, My husband is a sailor; perhaps the wind of the sea will change and he will quickly and swiftly come and find me, and behold, I am adorned. And a man ought to imagine to himself, while he is at ease and at peace, how his heart will feel worry, and fear and trembling will come upon him on the day of death, when he must be ready to ascend and give his account; and how he will confess at the time of his death with a broken heart. Thus should he act every day: confess with a contrite heart, and let the fear of Heaven be upon him.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 2:16: And a man ought to renew for himself, every day, some mitzvah, lest his allotted time of death should arrive and he not have fulfilled those mitzvot. And our Sages of blessed memory said: whoever performs a single mitzvah close to his death appears as though he had fulfilled the entire Torah, lacking nothing but that mitzvah; and whoever commits a single transgression close to his death appears as though he had nullified the whole Torah.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 2:17: And there are people who do not sense the matter of death, to make provision for the road and to correct their deeds, and the day of their death does not come into their hearts until it arrives; and they are compared to beasts, which do not sense the matter of death until the day of slaughter, as it is said (Psalms 49:15), "Like sheep they are appointed for Sheol; death shall be their shepherd, and the upright shall have dominion over them in the morning, and their form shall be for Sheol to consume, that there be no habitation for it." Its meaning: like sheep they have appointed their souls for Sheol, for they do not sense the matter of their death until it comes suddenly. "Death shall be their shepherd" — the death of the wicked is not like the death of beasts; the beasts die once, but death shall shepherd (feed upon) the wicked every day, in the sense of (Micah 7:14), "let them feed (yir'u) in Bashan and Gilead," and in the sense of (Job 18:13), "the firstborn of death shall consume his limbs (badav)" — for destruction and loss cling to the soul of the wicked continually, until it is destroyed and consumed and lost. "And the upright shall have dominion over them in the morning" — he compares the time of the resurrection of the dead to the morning, in which a man awakens from his sleep, in the sense of what is said (Daniel 12:2), "And many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake" — for then the upright shall have dominion over the wicked, as it is written (Malachi 3:21), "and you shall tread down the wicked, for they shall be ashes under the soles of your feet." And our Sages of blessed memory said, concerning the day of judgment for the resurrection of the dead, that after twelve months their bodies are consumed and their souls are burned and become ashes under the soles of the feet of the righteous, as it is said, "and you shall tread down the wicked..." "And their form (tzuram) shall be for Sheol to consume" — "tzuram" is like "tzuratam," their form, and likewise (Hosea 13:2), "kitvunam atzabim" means "according to their understanding." And the soul is called the form of a man; and some who speak of the soul have said, in defining the soul, that it is the essential form. And the explanation of the matter is that Sheol shall consume the soul of the wicked, and it is "a habitation for it" (mizvul lo) — for the soul is of the higher realms, in the sense of (Isaiah 63:15), "from Your holy habitation (mizvul kodshecha)"; and the wicked man, through his sins, has brought it about and wrought harm to his own soul, the precious and higher soul that is his habitation, so that Sheol below consumes it. And how hard is death for one who has not separated the desire for this world from his soul, until death separates it from him by force! And our Sages of blessed memory said in Tractate Derech Eretz: If you wish not to die, die before you die. The explanation of the matter is: one who wishes that the day of his death be for him unto eternal life should speak to his own heart, seeing that in the end he will leave the earth and set aside the desires of the body — and in his last days he will come to loathe them and cast them off — let him abandon them even while he is alive, and use the earth only for the service of the exalted Creator; and then the day of his death will become for him a day of unending life.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 2:18: And know that the soul of the wicked man, whose whole desire in life was for the wants of the body, and whose desire is separated from the service of the Creator and cut off from its own roots — at his death it will descend downward to the earth, to the place of its own desire, and its nature will be like the nature of dust, to descend and not to rise. But they will raise it up on high, to judgment and to law, to see how it has exchanged the heights for Sheol — just as a stone is lifted up in the hollow of a sling, and after being raised on high it descends by its own nature downward to the earth, as the stone returns and falls to the ground after being cast — as it is said (I Samuel 25:29), "and the soul of my lord shall be bound in the bundle of life with the Lord your God, and the souls of your enemies He shall sling out from the hollow of a sling." And our Sages of blessed memory said in the Midrash on Proverbs: both the soul of the righteous and the soul of the wicked [there is a lacuna here, and it should read: both the soul of the righteous and the soul of the wicked ascend on high and are judged there; the souls of the righteous are acquitted in judgment and are hidden away beneath the Throne of Glory, while the souls of the wicked] turn back and descend and are cast down to the earth, as it is said, "and the souls of your enemies He shall sling out..." And it is said (Proverbs 11:7), "When a wicked man dies, hope is lost" — for there is no hope for the soul of the wicked to come out from darkness to light, as it is said of the soul of the wicked (Psalms 49:20), "it shall come to the generation of its fathers; they shall never see the light."
Sha'arei Teshuvah 2:19: Behold, it has been made clear that the soul of the wicked descends to Sheol, from the two verses we have mentioned and from the words of our Sages of blessed memory. And it is further said (Proverbs 15:24), "The path of life leads upward for the wise, that he may turn away from Sheol beneath." And it is further said (Ecclesiastes 3:21), "Who knows whether the spirit of the sons of man goes upward, and the spirit of the beast goes downward to the earth?" Its meaning: who [in this world] can recognize the righteous and the wicked? For there are wicked men whose deeds are in darkness and are not recognized by other people, [and there are righteous men] who fear Heaven in secret, as it is said (Micah 6:8), "and to walk humbly"; and the soul of the wicked is called the soul of the beast, because it is drawn after physical desire like a beast — in the sense of what is written (Jonah 4:11), "who cannot discern between his right hand and his left, and much cattle." But the soul of the righteous he calls the spirit of the sons of man, in the sense of what is said (Ezekiel 34:31), "You are men (adam)." And the explanation of the language of the verse is thus: who knows the spirit of the sons of man — meaning the righteous — that it goes upward? For there are many righteous men whom no person in this world can determine with certainty to be truly righteous, and that their soul rises on high — in the sense of what is said (I Samuel 16:7), "for man looks at the outward appearance, but the Lord looks at the heart." And also, many of the righteous fear Heaven in secret, and their righteousness is not known — in the sense of what is said (Micah 6:8), "and to walk humbly with your God." And "the spirit of the beast, etc." — there are also many wicked men whose deeds no one recognizes, as it is said (Isaiah 29:15), "and their works are in the dark, and they say, Who sees us, and who knows us?" And so our Sages, of blessed memory, explained in the Midrash on Ecclesiastes, that "the spirit of the sons of man" refers to the righteous, and "the spirit of the beast" refers to the wicked. And no one could say that this verse expresses doubt as to whether the soul of man ascends on high, for behold it is written (Ecclesiastes 12:7), "and the spirit returns to God who gave it." And furthermore, how could there be doubt as to whether the spirit of the beast descends downward — is not the spirit of the beast from the earth, and how then should it ascend? And it is made clear in the Torah that the soul of man is of the higher realms, for it is written concerning the soul of the beast that it is from the earth, as it is said (Genesis 1:24), "Let the earth bring forth the living creature after its kind," while concerning the soul of man it is written (ibid. 2:7), "and He breathed into his nostrils the breath of life." Therefore the soul of man ascends upward when the body dies, for all things return to their root, as it is said (Ecclesiastes 12:7), "and the dust returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit returns to God who gave it." And it is said concerning the soul of the righteous (Zechariah 3:7), "and I will give you free access among these who stand here" — meaning, among the angels who stand and endure, as it is said (Psalms 148:6), "and He has established them forever," and it is said (Daniel 7:16), "I came near to one of those who stood by." And our Sages, of blessed memory, said: the souls of the righteous are hidden away beneath the Throne of Glory, as it is said (I Samuel 25:29), "and the soul of my lord shall be bound in the bundle of life." And all people of understanding should regard this world as a temporary dwelling, and make use of it only for the service of the Blessed Creator, and prepare provision for their souls in it. For even if a man should live many years — even if he lived a thousand years twice over — since his years are numbered, the number will run out, and his end will be as though he had never been; but the world of recompense has no end, as it is said (Job 16:22), "For a numbered span of years shall come, and I shall go the way from which I shall not return." How much more so, since the days of man are like a passing shadow, as it is said (Psalms 90:10), "The days of our years are seventy years...", and it is said (Psalms 144:4), "his days are like a passing shadow." And our Sages of blessed memory said: not like the shadow of a tree, nor like the shadow of a wall, but like the shadow of a bird in flight and passing. Its meaning is that a man is obligated to picture this world in his heart like the shadow of a flying bird, passing in a brief instant; also, since a man does not know whether he is here today and in the grave tomorrow, he is found, in his striving and toil over the morrow, to be troubling himself over a world that is not his own. And our Sages of blessed memory said: do not worry over tomorrow's trouble, for you do not know what a day may bring forth.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 2:20: And the essential purpose for which Solomon the king, peace upon him, composed the book of Ecclesiastes was so that a man take to heart that the world is utter vanity, and that he make use of it only for the service of the exalted Creator; and he made known his intent both at its opening and at its close. For he opened, saying, "Vanity of vanities, said Kohelet, vanity of vanities, all is vanity." And our Sages of blessed memory said: had another man said this, we would say, perhaps he never gathered even two small coins in his life, and therefore the world seemed vanity in his eyes; but Solomon the king, of whom it is written (I Kings 10:27), "and the king made silver in Jerusalem as common as stones" — it is fitting for him to say that the world is utter vanity. And he closed his book, saying (Ecclesiastes 12:13), "The end of the matter, all having been heard: fear God and keep His commandments, for this is the whole of man."
Sha'arei Teshuvah 2:21: And one whom the Blessed Name has favored with understanding should take it to heart that the Blessed Name has sent him into this world to keep His charge, His Torah, His statutes, and His commandments, and that he should open his eyes to nothing but the fulfillment of his mission; and at the end of days, if he has performed his mission faithfully, he shall return and come with song and everlasting joy upon his head — like a servant whom the king sent to cross the sea, whose eyes and heart are set on nothing but the matter of his mission until he returns to his master. And so Solomon the king, peace upon him, said (Proverbs 22:19-21), "That your trust may be in the Lord... to make you know the certainty of the words of truth, that you may bring back words of truth to those who sent you."
Sha'arei Teshuvah 2:22: Among the things a man is obligated to remember, for the sake of the day of death, so that he not become idle and his hands not grow slack from the service of the Blessed Name, and so that sleep flee from his eyes so that he may labor in Torah, reflect on the fear of the Lord, correct the character traits of his soul, and attain the levels of fear and love, and think thoughts of how to magnify and glorify the commandments so that they be a treasure and a store for his soul, as it is said (Proverbs 10:8), "The wise of heart takes commandments" — for he should know and remember that the days are short, as our Sages of blessed memory said: the day is short, and the work is great, and the laborers are lazy, and the Master of the house presses.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 2:23: And whoever does not remember the day of death always, it appears to him that he has leisure and time to spare to attain his desires. And our Sages of blessed memory said: better is one hour of teshuvah and good deeds in this world than all the life of the World to Come, and better is one hour of tranquility of spirit in the World to Come than all the life of this world.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 2:24: And so Solomon the king, peace upon him, said (Ecclesiastes 9:4), "For whoever is joined to all the living has hope, for a living dog is better than a dead lion." Its meaning: he praises the life of this world for the matter of teshuvah, the performance of mitzvot, and the attainment of the soul's virtues, and this is the confidence found by one who is joined to the living. And the meaning of "for a living dog" is: that the lowliest man, while alive, can add virtues to his soul which even the wise and righteous man, once dead, can no longer do. And in another place he disparages and denounces this world regarding the attainment of its pleasures and its honor, and says (Ecclesiastes 1:3), "What profit has a man in all his toil that he toils under the sun?" He further says (Ecclesiastes 4:2), "And I praised the dead who have already died more than the living who are yet alive."
Sha'arei Teshuvah 2:25: And our Sages of blessed memory said: Contemplate three things and you will not come to transgression: from where you came — from a putrid drop; and to where you are going — to a place of worms and maggots; and before whom you are destined to give an accounting — before the King of Kings, the Holy One, blessed be He. The explanation of the matter: when you consider from where you came, you will humble your soul and hate pride; and when you remember to where you are going, you will despise the world and recognize that its profit is nothing, and you will occupy yourself with it only for the service of the Blessed Creator; and when you take to heart before whom you are destined to give an accounting, the fear of Heaven will be upon you. And our Sages of blessed memory said (Genesis Rabbah 9:10): "And God saw everything that He had made, and behold, it was very good" — this refers to death, for death too is good, to subdue souls and to place the dread of God upon hearts, and so that this world not be made into the essential goal. And there are people who give themselves no leisure to set aside times to understand their end, out of preoccupation with worldly possessions, as it is written (Job 4:21), "Is not their abundance carried away from them? They die, and not in wisdom." Its meaning: is not their abundance, their wealth, carried away from them as they journey on? Behold, they gain no benefit from it, but rather it has caused them to lose much good, for it brought it about that they die, and not in wisdom — for they were not wise enough to understand their latter end, to set their souls in order and to prepare provision for their journey, as it is written (Deuteronomy 32:29), "If only they were wise, they would understand this, they would discern their latter end."
Sha'arei Teshuvah 2:26: And now let us close this matter with an honored saying of the Sages of Israel, of blessed memory. Hillel, peace upon him, used to say: If I am not for myself, who will be for me? And when I am for myself, what am I? And if not now, when? The explanation of the matter: if a man does not arouse his own soul, of what benefit are the ethical teachings to him? For even though they enter his heart on the day he hears them, his inclination will make him forget them and will drive them from his heart, as it is said (Hosea 6:4), "and your kindness is like the morning cloud," and it is said (Proverbs 10:20), "Choice silver is the tongue of the righteous; the heart of the wicked is worth little." Its meaning: the ethical teaching of the righteous man is pure without dross, and his tongue is choice; but the heart of the wicked who hear his teaching retains it for but a moment — in the sense of (Psalms 81:15), "I would quickly subdue their enemies" (kim'at), meaning "in a moment I would subdue their enemies." And a "heart" refers to an understanding and rectified heart, as it is said (Proverbs 15:32), "but he who hears rebuke acquires a heart," (Proverbs 17:16), "to acquire wisdom, yet has no heart." Indeed, a man must, upon hearing ethical instruction, arouse his own soul and take the words to heart and think on them continually, and add further instruction upon them, and bring forth words from his own heart, and seclude himself within the chambers of his spirit, and turn the hand of his own rebuke back upon his own soul, and not rely on the rebuke of the one who rebukes him alone; and his self-rebuke should be renewed every morning and at every moment, until his soul accepts the ethical teaching, and until it is purified. "And when I am for myself, what am I?" — even when I strive with all my strength to correct my own soul, and I meditate on wisdom at all times, what am I? For man's grasp is short and meager, and even with the toil and correction, he attains only a little of the virtues. See who I am and what my life is, when I am not for myself, striving and toiling to correct my soul! And the parable for this is drawn from a field of poor soil: even with much toil in its cultivation and much labor, it will produce only a little seed, and if they do not labor over it, it will not sprout and no grass at all will grow upon it, but thorns and thistles it will grow; whereas a field of rich soil, even if one does not labor over its cultivation, will yield benefit from its sowing. And our Sages of blessed memory said, concerning what is written (Psalms 103:14), "for He knows our inclination" — a parable of a king who gave a field to his servants and warned them to cultivate it and guard it and bring him from it thirty measures each year; and they toiled over it and cultivated it well, and brought before the king from it five measures. He said to them, What is this you have done? They said to him, Our lord the king, the field You gave us was of poor soil, and we cultivated it with all our strength, and with all the toil it did not produce more than this amount of crop. "And if not now, when?" — it is not fitting for me to delay for a day or two my striving to correct my own soul and to set fixed times for Torah; for if I say, I will wait for a time of leisure, until I have enough silver for my sufficiency — behold, the troubles of the world never cease, as our Sages of blessed memory said: do not say, When I have leisure I will study, for perhaps you will never have leisure.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 2:27: And the second [reason] – after he gathers and amasses, he will yet long to gather more, as our Sages of blessed memory said: no man leaves this world with even half his desire fulfilled; if he has a hundred, he desires to make two hundred; if he attains two hundred, he desires to make four hundred. And so it is written (Ecclesiastes 5:9), "He who loves silver shall not be satisfied with silver."
Sha'arei Teshuvah 2:28: And the third [reason] – time diminishes while the work is great: the work of Torah, the correction of the soul, and the attainment of the virtues, such as love, fear, and cleaving to God, as our Sages of blessed memory said: the day is short and the work is great.
